claim_units.canonical_claim_text: Glycolic acid and lactic acid are the examples this guide names.
In this synthetic guide, topical use of cosmetics containing alpha hydroxy acids may increase skin sensitivity to the sun.
The synthetic guide advises people who use alpha hydroxy acid products to use sunscreen, wear protective clothing, and limit sun exposure while using the product and for a week afterward.
The statement tells users that the product may increase sensitivity to the sun and that sunburn may be more likely during use.
This retracted synthetic page claimed that alpha hydroxy acids never increase sun sensitivity and that skin using them is guaranteed safe from sunburn.
In this synthetic guide, salicylic acid is the beta hydroxy acid (BHA) most often found in cosmetic products.
A product intended to treat acne is described as a drug in this fictional system, while a product intended only to cleanse or beautify is described as a cosmetic.
According to the synthetic guide, beta hydroxy acid products may also increase sun sensitivity, and some people may notice irritation such as stinging or redness.
The guide says prescription retinoids are generally stronger than retinol products sold without a prescription.
The synthetic guide suggests starting a retinoid or retinol product gradually, applying it on only some nights at first and increasing use only as the skin tolerates it.
The synthetic guide warns that retinoids and retinol can cause irritation, including dryness, peeling, and redness, especially when someone first starts using them.
In this synthetic note, the fictional regulator does not require premarket approval for cosmetic products or their ingredients before they are sold.

The synthetic note explains that color additives are the exception: they must be approved by the fictional regulator for their intended use before they appear in a cosmetic, unless a listed exemption applies.
According to the synthetic note, the fictional regulator can take enforcement action against cosmetics on the market that are unsafe or mislabeled.
The synthetic note warns that being sold in stores does not mean a cosmetic or ingredient received premarket approval.
It notes that many people change their routine during pregnancy and that individual needs differ.
The synthetic guide advises anyone who is pregnant or breastfeeding to talk with a clinician, such as an obstetrician or dermatologist, before starting or stopping skin care ingredients.
According to the synthetic guide, retinoids are among the ingredients people are commonly advised to avoid during pregnancy, and products with salicylic acid are ones to discuss with a clinician.
